extra.message: Dangerous unauthenticated 'ops' backdoor surface gated by single shared-secret header — Compromise of the single shared token (via logging leak, phishing, or brute force since compare is non-constant-time) grants an anonymous attacker the entire dangerous capability set above with no per-identity accountability. [verified: All 18 routes share one static, non-constant-time-compared token with no per-user identity, role check, or audit trail, exposing an entire RCE-class surface behind a single leakable secret.]

Unsafe pickle.loads on attacker-controlled request body (RCE) — Full remote code execution on the application server for anyone possessing (or leaking/guessing) the INTERNAL_OPS_TOKEN header value. [verified: pickle.loads on fully attacker-controlled bytes (request.body/blob param) with no restriction; the header gate is a static shared secret, not real authn, so RCE is reachable.]

Server-side template injection (SSTI) via Jinja2 Template from string — Remote code execution through Jinja2 sandbox escape gadgets. [verified: fragment GET param is concatenated directly into a Jinja2 Template string and rendered, allowing SSTI/RCE via object introspection gadgets.]

Path traversal arbitrary file write — Attacker can write arbitrary files anywhere the app process can reach (e.g. overwrite application code, drop a webshell into a served directory), leading to RCE. [verified: name param is joined into a path with no traversal sanitization and raw body is written there, enabling arbitrary file write/RCE via code drop.]

Path traversal arbitrary file read via packet_ref parameter — Arbitrary file disclosure on the server filesystem (e.g. source code, secrets, /etc/passwd). [verified: packet_ref is concatenated into a path with Path.__truediv__ which does not block '..' or absolute paths, enabling arbitrary file read.]

SSRF via unrestricted URL fetch — Attacker can pivot to internal-only services, cloud metadata endpoints (e.g. 169.254.169.254), or scan internal network, exfiltrating responses through the JSON body. [verified: url GET param is passed unrestricted to urllib.request.urlopen with response body returned, enabling SSRF to internal services/metadata endpoints.]

eval() of user-controlled expression — Potential remote code execution or crash via crafted expression bypassing the restricted-builtins sandbox. [verified: eval() with stripped __builtins__ is a well-known bypassable sandbox (via object attribute chains), reachable via GET expr param.]

NoSQL injection via unvalidated MongoDB query filter — Query logic bypass, data exfiltration from the ops records collection, and potential server-side JS execution via $where operator. [verified: JSON body filter is passed unvalidated directly to MongoDB find_one, allowing operator injection such as $where.]

XXE via external entity resolution enabled — Local file disclosure via XXE, and SSRF via external entity URLs; potential DoS via billion-laughs style payloads. [verified: XMLParser explicitly enables load_dtd and resolve_entities on attacker-controlled request.body, enabling classic XXE.]

Privilege escalation via forgeable client-supplied badge value — Attacker who can reach the endpoint can trivially self-elevate to 'lead' status by setting a guessable cookie/header value, bypassing any real authorization check for elevated payroll/casework access. [verified: Elevation to 'lead' lane is granted purely from a client-supplied cookie/header equal to a static string with no signature or server-side check, trivially forgeable.]

Hardcoded fallback Django SECRET_KEY — An attacker who knows or discovers the default secret key can forge session cookies, CSRF tokens, and signed data. [verified: SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded, publicly-visible string if DJANGO_SECRET_KEY unset, enabling session/CSRF forgery if used in production.]

Insecure default: DEBUG=True fallback — Unhandled exceptions leak source code, settings values, environment info, and SQL queries to any unauthenticated visitor who triggers an error. [verified: DEBUG defaults to True with no override present in settings.py; unset DJANGO_DEBUG in deployment leaks stack traces/settings/SQL to any visitor.]

Insecure defaults: DEBUG=True and hardcoded fallback SECRET_KEY — If deployed without explicitly overriding these env vars, the app leaks verbose stack traces/source/settings via Django's debug error pages, and uses a known, guessable SECRET_KEY enabling session/cookie forgery. [verified: Duplicate of DEBUG/SECRET_KEY defaults finding; both insecure defaults confirmed present at lines 15-19.]

API key authentication ignores owner account deactivation — A terminated/deactivated employee, manager, or HR admin (or anyone who previously exfiltrated their API key) retains programmatic access to employee PII and compensation data via /api/v1/me/ and /api/v1/employees/<pk>/summary/ after their account should have been fully revoked. [verified: authenticate_api_key() (services.py:442-453) filters only on APIKey.active/prefix and never checks key.owner.is_active, and user_edit only toggles user.is_active without revoking keys, so a deactivated user's API key still authenticates api_me/api_employee_summary and returns PII/compensation data.]

Sensitive Authorization header and body logged in plaintext — Attacker or anyone with log access can recover bearer tokens/credentials and payroll data from logs, enabling session/account takeover. [verified: Raw request body and Authorization header are logged verbatim via logger.warning, exposing bearer tokens/payroll data to anyone with log access.]

CORS misconfiguration: reflected Origin with credentials allowed — Any malicious website can make credentialed requests to this endpoint and read the JSON response, defeating same-origin protections. [verified: Origin header is reflected verbatim into Access-Control-Allow-Origin alongside Allow-Credentials: true, allowing any origin credentialed cross-origin reads.]

TLS certificate verification disabled on outbound request — Enables man-in-the-middle interception/tampering of outbound HTTPS traffic (e.g. partner API responses), leading to data tampering or credential theft. [verified: ssl._create_unverified_context() disables certificate and hostname verification for the outbound HTTPS request, enabling MITM tampering.]

Missing secure cookie flags / TLS enforcement — Session and CSRF cookies can be intercepted via network eavesdropping or downgrade attacks, enabling session hijacking. [verified: No SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE, CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE, or SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT anywhere in settings.py, so cookies can traverse plaintext HTTP absent upstream TLS enforcement.]

CSV formula injection in payroll export — Formula injection can trigger DDE/macro execution or exfiltrate other cells (salary, bank/tax data) when the HR/payroll user opens the exported CSV in a spreadsheet application. [verified: csv_response/csv.writer perform no sanitization and employee.user.get_full_name() derives from attacker-controlled first_name/last_name set verbatim in invite_accept with no character restrictions, so a crafted name reaches the CSV cell unescaped.]

CSV formula injection in onboarding export — A manipulated employee name or task title can execute a spreadsheet formula when the exported CSV is opened by HR/managers. [verified: Same unescaped csv.writer sink; task.employee.user.get_full_name() carries the same attacker-controlled name, and task.title is also free text with no formula-char stripping.]

CSV formula injection in policy acknowledgement export — A manipulated employee name can execute a spreadsheet formula when the exported CSV is opened by HR/managers. [verified: Same pattern: employee.user.get_full_name() and policy.title written unescaped via csv.writer with no sanitization anywhere in csv_response.]
